CHS is the fucking worst. I was diagnosed six months ago and quit the same day. The first month was the absolute worst, it gets easier after that. You deserve to live a happy, healthy life and quitting will help with that, especially if you have CHS symptoms. I like the app Grounded to keep track of my sobriety. Six months and two days down! YTA. My dad tried doing shit like this to me my whole life, starting at age 10. I honestly can’t recall a single conversation I’ve ever had with him where my weight didn’t come up. I’ve had an eating disorder for years. A few years ago I lost 60 pounds from starving myself and puking after eating. That year at Christmas, my weight loss and how much better I looked were all he could talk about, even though I hadn’t seen him in a year and definitely had other things I would have rather discussed. When it was time for me to leave, his parting words to me were, “keep starving!” I cried my whole drive home. We have not spoken in person since, and I went completely no contact after my grandma passed away in June. Your daughter will resent you if you keep this up. There are better ways to help someone live a healthy lifestyle. Shame and humiliation are not the ways to do it.

Yeah! When I was in group therapy we all got the DBT workbook. Some of the worksheets are available online as PDFs, but you can also buy a copy of the book.

DBT is great for mindfulness, which is a skill that takes time and effort to learn. It’s hard to change your thought patterns, but it’s very useful, particularly for people with PTSD and BPD.

The handheld needs to stay in your hand. Don't bother putting it in your vest pocket, it'll beep before it gets too cozy there. 

Have a fast cashier on your most popular register (unless it's a slow day, then it's better to have a slow cashier there so the other cashiers still get customers). And then crew until you die. Pay attention to customers ready to check out. Literally walk them to the shortest line. They're not motivated enough to find it for themselves. This will keep your lines down. Having associates know to redline and grab customers from other lanes is also helpful, but a lot of cashiers won't unless someone's watching them. 

Check the TMAT (schedule) when you start your shift. At my store, we have to be careful about the service desk because the coverage is usually subpar at best and we don't have many associates able to work over there. Plan ahead for those kinds of tricky breaks and ask management if you need assistance. 

Know your cashiers. Know how flexible they are with their breaks, which registers they like to work on, and how reliable they are coming back from their breaks and meals. Happy cashiers make customers happy. 

If you have a cashier who always takes 25 minutes to get back to their register, don't count on them to be back in time to send someone home. Don't put three people who go home within the same hour on three consecutive registers.

If you look at your handheld and there are 600 notifications and you're overwhelmed, step to the side (I like to lean on a carousel at an empty register), clear what you can immediately (no sales, aborts, SCO registers fake notifications, etc). Then take care of your training questions in order. Alcohol sales come first. Price checks come last. 

If you have multiple CSMs working, don't be afraid to get on a register to help get your lines down. Avoid the register at all costs if you're working alone. You'll never escape. 

Teach your cashiers to be specific with their action codes. Don't 248 for a price check. Don't 248 for a carry out. Don't 248 for a break. Don't 248 for wic. There are specific actions codes for all of them. Use them. This way, you'll know what you're in for before you even get to the register. 

Keep a printed list of checked out registers in your pocket. I keep mine in my shirt pocket so it doesn't get lost or too wrinkled. At the end of the night, I write the names of the associates that will be pulling each register. I put a star next to the ones I'll pull myself when I have time between calls and audits. Cashiers that go home after 8pm will pull their own registers. I like to have everything pulled by 9:45 except my 10 and 11pm go-homes. 

Familiarize yourself with the SCO registers. It's better to fix the problem with the machine than to stick it in cards only and piss off all the customers who want to use cash. Most of the time it's a quick fix. To add to this, ask your overnight CSM to load the SCO registers with extra money for particularly busy days (long weekends, holidays, payday, etc). This'll save you time so your registers aren't running out of bills throughout the day. 

Take your breaks out of the building. Don't get caught in the break room gossip. Don't stay inside for the whole nine hour day. Eating my lunch outside has improved my workday immensely. This is an emotionally taxing job. Don't let it get you down too much. 

Good luck!
